description: Self-balancing BSTs decomposed. AVL, red-black, splay, and treap. The shared machinery: rotations (the structural primitive), invariants (what keeps the height bounded), and rebalancing (how to restore the invariant after modification). Each variant trades implementation complexity, balance tightness, and amortised guarantees differently.

sub_mechanisms.name: BST_property
sub_mechanisms.definition: For each node x: all keys in left subtree < x.key < all keys in right subtree. The fundamental BST invariant.
sub_mechanisms.why: Lets search proceed by comparison: if target < node, go left; else right. The property must be preserved by all operations. Rotations preserve it because they preserve in-order traversal.

sub_mechanisms.name: left_rotation
sub_mechanisms.definition: Rotate right child up: y becomes x's parent; x becomes y's left child; y's old left becomes x's new right. 3 pointer updates.
sub_mechanisms.why: Lowers x by one level, raises y by one level. Preserves the BST property (the in-order order remains the same). The atomic move for rebalancing.

sub_mechanisms.name: right_rotation
sub_mechanisms.definition: Mirror of left rotation: y is x's left child; y becomes x's parent; x becomes y's right child; y's old right becomes x's new left.
sub_mechanisms.why: Together with left rotation, rotations form the complete set of local rebalancing primitives. Any rebalancing in AVL or red-black is a sequence of these rotations.

sub_mechanisms.name: AVL_balance_factor
sub_mechanisms.definition: Per-node integer: height(right subtree) − height(left subtree). AVL invariant: |balance_factor| ≤ 1 for every node.
sub_mechanisms.why: Tight balance: heights differ by at most 1 means tree depth is at most 1.44 log n. Fastest possible BST lookup. Cost: more rotations on insert/delete than red-black.

sub_mechanisms.name: AVL_rebalance
sub_mechanisms.definition: On insert/delete, walk up from the modified node. If a node's balance factor becomes ±2, perform 1 or 2 rotations to restore ≤ 1.
sub_mechanisms.why: Four cases (LL, LR, RL, RR) covering left-heavy and right-heavy imbalance. Each is a single or double rotation. After rebalancing one level, the balance factor change propagates up — at most O(log n) rotations per insert/delete.

sub_mechanisms.name: red_black_coloring
sub_mechanisms.definition: Each node is red or black. Rules: root is black; red nodes have black children (no red-red); every root-to-leaf path has the same number of black nodes.
sub_mechanisms.why: Looser balance than AVL: longest path ≤ 2 × shortest path. Less aggressive rebalancing. Easier to recover from deletion than AVL.

sub_mechanisms.name: red_black_insert_fixup
sub_mechanisms.definition: Insert as red. If parent is red (red-red violation), recolor + possibly rotate. Cases depend on uncle's color.
sub_mechanisms.why: Three cases handle the various red-red configurations. Each is O(1) work; the walk up the tree is O(log n). Standard textbook (CLRS) details all cases.

sub_mechanisms.name: red_black_delete_fixup
sub_mechanisms.definition: Delete + replace as in plain BST. If the deleted/replaced node was black, walk up restoring the black-height invariant via recoloring + rotations.
sub_mechanisms.why: More complex than insert: must restore the equal-black-nodes-per-path property. ~6 cases. The complexity is why red-black is famously hard to implement correctly. Once implemented, it's a workhorse.

sub_mechanisms.name: splay_tree
sub_mechanisms.definition: On every access, splay (rotate) the accessed node to the root via zig, zig-zig, zig-zag operations.
sub_mechanisms.why: Self-adjusting: frequently accessed nodes stay near the root. Amortised O(log n) per operation. Excellent for skewed access distributions; competitive with optimal static BST.

sub_mechanisms.name: treap
sub_mechanisms.definition: BST + heap. Each node has key (BST property) + random priority (heap property: parent priority ≥ child priority). Inserts as BST leaf, then rotate up to restore heap.
sub_mechanisms.why: Randomisation gives expected O(log n) operations without explicit balancing logic. Conceptually simpler than red-black or AVL. Used in functional data structures, persistent variants.

sub_mechanisms.name: successor_predecessor
sub_mechanisms.definition: In-order successor of node x: smallest key > x.key. Either leftmost node of x's right subtree, or the lowest ancestor where x is in the left subtree.
sub_mechanisms.why: Used by deletion when removing a node with two children: replace with successor, then delete the successor. The standard BST deletion algorithm.

derivation_rules.name: rotations_preserve_BST_property
if: a left or right rotation is applied
then: the in-order traversal is unchanged and the BST property holds
derivation_rules.why: Rotations move subtrees around but preserve which keys are < or > others. Mechanical proof: trace pointer updates + verify each subtree's keys still satisfy the property at every node. The structural foundation of self-balancing.

derivation_rules.name: AVL_strictest_balance_fastest_lookup
then: tree height is at most ~1.44 log n
derivation_rules.why: Fibonacci-like recurrence on minimum nodes per height. AVL has tightest balance among practical BSTs → fastest lookup. Trade-off: more rotations on writes than red-black.

derivation_rules.name: red_black_height_at_most_2_log_n_plus_1
derivation_rules.why: Black-height is log n; each path alternates at most every-other-red. Looser than AVL but still O(log n). Standard textbook proof.

derivation_rules.name: splay_competitive_with_optimal_static
then: splay tree's total work is within constant factor of optimal offline BST
derivation_rules.why: Splay's dynamic-optimality conjecture is the famous open question. Proven within constant factor of working-set bound. Self-adjusting structure adapts to actual access pattern without knowing it in advance.

derivation_rules.name: treap_expected_log_n_via_randomisation
then: expected tree height is O(log n)
derivation_rules.why: Random heap order is equivalent to inserting nodes in random key order. Expected depth analysis of random BST gives O(log n). No worst-case guarantee (a malicious random source could give O(n)), but expected behaviour is robust.
